By and by, through the glass the stranger’s boats and manned mast-heads proved her a whale-ship. But as she was so far to windward, and shooting by, apparently making a passage to some other ground, the Pequod could not hope to reach her. So the signal was set to see what response would be made.

Thereby, the whale commanders are enabled to recognise each other upon the ocean, even at considerable distances and with no small facility.

The Pequod’s signal was at last responded to by the stranger’s setting her own; which proved the ship to be the Jeroboam of Nantucket. Squaring her yards, she bore down, ranged abeam under the Pequod’s lee, and lowered a boat; it soon drew nigh; but, as the side-ladder was being rigged by Starbuck’s order to accommodate the visiting captain, the stranger in question waved his hand from his boat’s stern in token of that proceeding being entirely unnecessary. It turned out that the Jeroboam had a malignant epidemic on board, and that Mayhew, her captain, was fearful of infecting the Pequod’s company. For, though himself and boat’s crew remained untainted, and though his ship was half a rifle-shot off, and an incorruptible sea and air rolling and flowing between; yet conscientiously adhering to the timid quarantine of the land, he peremptorily refused to come into direct contact with the Pequod.

But this did by no means prevent all communications. Preserving an interval of some few yards between itself and the ship, the Jeroboam’s boat by the occasional use of its oars contrived to keep parallel to the Pequod, as she heavily forged through the sea (for by this time it blew very fresh), with her main-topsail aback; though, indeed, at times by the sudden onset of a large rolling wave, the boat would be pushed some way ahead; but would be soon skilfully brought to her proper bearings again. Subject to this, and other the like interruptions now and then, a conversation was sustained between the two parties; but at intervals not without still another interruption of a very different sort.

Pulling an oar in the Jeroboam’s boat, was a man of a singular appearance, even in that wild whaling life where individual notabilities make up all totalities. He was a small, short, youngish man, sprinkled all over his face with freckles, and wearing redundant yellow hair. A long-skirted, cabalistically-cut coat of a faded walnut tinge enveloped him; the overlapping sleeves of which were rolled up on his wrists. A deep, settled, fanatic delirium was in his eyes.

So soon as this figure had been first descried, Stubb had exclaimed—“That’s he! that’s he!—the long-togged scaramouch the Town-Ho’s company told us of!” Stubb here alluded to a strange story told of the Jeroboam, and a certain man among her crew, some time previous when the Pequod spoke the Town-Ho. According to this account and what was subsequently learned, it seemed that the scaramouch in question had gained a wonderful ascendency over almost everybody in the Jeroboam. His story was this:

He had been originally nurtured among the crazy society of Neskyeuna Shakers, where he had been a great prophet; in their cracked, secret meetings having several times descended from heaven by the way of a trap-door, announcing the speedy opening of the seventh vial, which he carried in his vest-pocket; but, which, instead of containing gunpowder, was supposed to be charged with laudanum. A strange, apostolic whim having seized him, he had left Neskyeuna for Nantucket, where, with that cunning peculiar to craziness, he assumed a steady, common-sense exterior, and offered himself as a green-hand candidate for the Jeroboam’s whaling voyage. They engaged him; but straightway upon the ship’s getting out of sight of land, his insanity broke out in a freshet. He announced himself as the archangel Gabriel, and commanded the captain to jump overboard. He published his manifesto, whereby he set himself forth as the deliverer of the isles of the sea and vicar-general of all Oceanica. The unflinching earnestness with which he declared these things;—the dark, daring play of his sleepless, excited imagination, and all the preternatural terrors of real delirium, united to invest this Gabriel in the minds of the majority of the ignorant crew, with an atmosphere of sacredness. Moreover, they were afraid of him. As such a man, however, was not of much practical use in the ship, especially as he refused to work except when he pleased, the incredulous captain would fain have been rid of him; but apprised that that individual’s intention was to land him in the first convenient port, the archangel forthwith opened all his seals and vials—devoting the ship and all hands to unconditional perdition, in case this intention was carried out. So strongly did he work upon his disciples among the crew, that at last in a body they went to the captain and told him if Gabriel was sent from the ship, not a man of them would remain. He was therefore forced to relinquish his plan. Nor would they permit Gabriel to be any way maltreated, say or do what he would; so that it came to pass that Gabriel had the complete freedom of the ship. The consequence of all this was, that the archangel cared little or nothing for the captain and mates; and since the epidemic had broken out, he carried a higher hand than ever; declaring that the plague, as he called it, was at his sole command; nor should it be stayed but according to his good pleasure. The sailors, mostly poor devils, cringed, and some of them fawned before him; in obedience to his instructions, sometimes rendering him personal homage, as to a god. Such things may seem incredible; but, however wondrous, they are true. Nor is the history of fanatics half so striking in respect to the measureless self-deception of the fanatic himself, as his measureless power of deceiving and bedevilling so many others. But it is time to return to the Pequod.
“I fear not thy epidemic, man,” said Ahab from the bulwarks, to Captain Mayhew, who stood in the boat’s stern; “come on board.”
But now Gabriel started to his feet.
“Think, think of the fevers, yellow and bilious! Beware of the horrible plague!”
“Gabriel! Gabriel!” cried Captain Mayhew; “thou must either—” But that instant a headlong wave shot the boat far ahead, and its seethings drowned all speech.
“Hast thou seen the White Whale?” demanded Ahab, when the boat drifted back.
“Think, think of thy whale-boat, stoven and sunk! Beware of the horrible tail!”

“I tell thee again, Gabriel, that—” But again the boat tore ahead as if dragged by fiends. Nothing was said for some moments, while a succession of riotous waves rolled by, which by one of those occasional caprices of the seas were tumbling, not heaving it. Meantime, the hoisted sperm whale’s head jogged about very violently, and Gabriel was seen eyeing it with rather more apprehensiveness than his archangel nature seemed to warrant.

When this interlude was over, Captain Mayhew began a dark story concerning Moby Dick; not, however, without frequent interruptions from Gabriel, whenever his name was mentioned, and the crazy sea that seemed leagued with him.

It seemed that the Jeroboam had not long left home, when upon speaking a whale-ship, her people were reliably apprised of the existence of Moby Dick, and the havoc he had made. Greedily sucking in this intelligence, Gabriel solemnly warned the captain against attacking the White Whale, in case the monster should be seen; in his gibbering insanity, pronouncing the White Whale to be no less a being than the Shaker God incarnated; the Shakers receiving the Bible. But when, some year or two afterwards, Moby Dick was fairly sighted from the mast-heads, Macey, the chief mate, burned with ardour to encounter him; and the captain himself being not unwilling to let him have the opportunity, despite all the archangel’s denunciations and forewarnings, Macey succeeded in persuading five men to man his boat. With them he pushed off; and, after much weary pulling, and many perilous, unsuccessful onsets, he at last succeeded in getting one iron fast. Meantime, Gabriel, ascending to the main-royal mast-head, was tossing one arm in frantic gestures, and hurling forth prophecies of speedy doom to the sacrilegious assailants of his divinity. Now, while Macey, the mate, was standing up in his boat’s bow, and with all the reckless energy of his tribe was venting his wild exclamations upon the whale, and essaying to get a fair chance for his poised lance, lo! a broad white shadow rose from the sea; by its quick, fanning motion, temporarily taking the breath out of the bodies of the oarsmen. Next instant, the luckless mate, so full of furious life, was smitten bodily into the air, and making a long arc in his descent, fell into the sea at the distance of about fifty yards. Not a chip of the boat was harmed, nor a hair of any oarsman’s head; but the mate for ever sank.

It is well to parenthesize here, that of the fatal accidents in the Sperm-Whale Fishery, this kind is perhaps almost as frequent as any. Sometimes, nothing is injured but the man who is thus annihilated; oftener the boat’s bow is knocked off, or the thigh-board, in which the headsman stands, is torn from its place and accompanies the body. But strangest of all is the circumstance, that in more instances than one, when the body has been recovered, not a single mark of violence is discernible; the man being stark dead.

The whole calamity, with the falling form of Macey, was plainly descried from the ship. Raising a piercing shriek—“The vial! the vial!” Gabriel called off the terror-stricken crew from the further hunting of the whale. This terrible event clothed the archangel with added influence; because his credulous disciples believed that he had specifically fore-announced it, instead of only making a general prophecy, which any one might have done, and so have chanced to hit one of many marks in the wide margin allowed. He became a nameless terror to the ship.

Mayhew having concluded his narration, Ahab put such questions to him, that the stranger captain could not forbear inquiring whether he intended to hunt the White Whale, if opportunity should offer. To which Ahab answered—“Aye.” Straightway, then, Gabriel once more started to his feet, glaring upon the old man, and vehemently exclaimed, with downward pointed finger—“Think, think of the blasphemer—dead, and down there!—beware of the blasphemer’s end!”

Then Gabriel shrieked out to his comrades to give way with their oars, and in that manner the mutinous boat rapidly shot away from the Pequod.
As, after this interlude, the seamen resumed their work upon the jacket of the whale, many strange things were hinted in reference to this wild affair.

"I'm not afraid of your epidemic, man," said Ahab from the bulwarks to Captain Mayhew, who stood in the boat's stern. "Come on board."
But now Gabriel started to his feet.
"Think, think of the fevers, yellow and bilious! Beware of the horrible plague!"
"Gabriel! Gabriel!" cried Captain Mayhew. "You must either —" But that instant a headlong wave shot the boat far ahead, and its noise drowned all speech.
"Have you seen the White Whale?" demanded Ahab, when the boat drifted back.
"Think, think of your whale-boat, stoven and sunk! Beware of the horrible tail!"

"I tell you again, Gabriel, that —" But once more the boat shot ahead as if fiends were dragging it. For some moments no one spoke, while a series of riotous waves rolled past — waves that, in one of the sea's occasional whims, were tumbling the boat rather than lifting it. Meanwhile the hoisted sperm whale's head was jolting about violently, and Gabriel could be seen eyeing it with rather more alarm than his archangel nature seemed to justify.

When this interlude was over, Captain Mayhew began a dark story about Moby Dick — not, however, without frequent interruptions from Gabriel whenever his name was mentioned, and from the crazy sea that seemed to be in league with him.

It seemed that the Jeroboam had not long left home when, on speaking a whale-ship, her people were reliably informed of the existence of Moby Dick and the havoc he had made. Greedily drinking in this news, Gabriel solemnly warned the captain against attacking the White Whale in case the monster should be seen; in his gibbering insanity he declared the White Whale to be no less a being than the Shaker God incarnate, the Shakers accepting the Bible. But when, a year or two afterward, Moby Dick was fairly sighted from the mastheads, Macey, the chief mate, burned with eagerness to encounter him; and the captain himself being not unwilling to give him the chance, despite all the archangel's denunciations and warnings, Macey succeeded in persuading five men to man his boat. With them he pushed off; and after much weary pulling, and many perilous, unsuccessful attacks, he at last succeeded in getting one iron fast. Meanwhile Gabriel, climbing to the main-royal masthead, was tossing one arm in frantic gestures and hurling forth prophecies of swift doom upon the sacrilegious attackers of his divinity. Now, while Macey the mate was standing up in his boat's bow, and with all the reckless energy of his tribe was venting his wild exclamations at the whale and trying to get a fair chance for his poised lance — look! a broad white shadow rose from the sea, and by its quick, fanning motion for the moment knocked the breath out of the oarsmen's bodies. The next instant the luckless mate, so full of furious life, was struck bodily into the air, and, making a long arc in his descent, fell into the sea about fifty yards away. Not a chip of the boat was harmed, nor a hair of any oarsman's head; but the mate sank forever.

It is worth adding here, in parentheses, that among the fatal accidents of the Sperm-Whale Fishery, this kind is perhaps nearly as common as any. Sometimes nothing is hurt except the man who is wiped out this way; more often the bow of the boat is knocked off, or the thigh-board where the headsman (the officer commanding the boat) stands is torn loose and goes along with the body. But strangest of all is the fact that more than once, when the body has been recovered, not a single mark of violence could be found on it — and yet the man was stone dead.

From the ship the whole disaster, including Macey's falling body, was clearly visible. With a piercing shriek — "The vial! the vial!" — Gabriel called the terrified crew off from any further pursuit of the whale. This terrible event gave the archangel still more influence, because his gullible disciples believed he had predicted this very thing, rather than having merely made a general prophecy, which anyone could have done, and so happened to hit one of the many targets its wide margin allowed. He became a nameless terror to the ship.

When Mayhew had finished his story, Ahab put such questions to him that the stranger captain could not help asking whether he intended to hunt the White Whale, if the opportunity came. To which Ahab answered — "Aye." Immediately, then, Gabriel once more started to his feet, glaring at the old man, and vehemently exclaimed, with downward-pointing finger — "Think, think of the blasphemer — dead, and down there! — beware of the blasphemer's end!"
Ahab stolidly turned aside, then said to Mayhew, "Captain, I have just remembered my letter-bag. There is a letter for one of your officers, if I'm not mistaken. Starbuck, look through the bag."

Every whale-ship carries out a good number of letters for various other ships, and whether they reach the people they are addressed to depends purely on the chance of meeting those ships somewhere in the four oceans. So most letters never arrive; and many are received only when they are two or three years old or more.

Soon Starbuck returned with a letter in his hand. It was badly creased, damp, and covered with a dull, spotted green mold from being kept in a dark locker in the cabin. Of such a letter, Death himself might well have been the postman.

"Can't you read it?" cried Ahab. "Give it to me, man. Aye, aye, it's but a dim scrawl — what's this?" As he was studying it out, Starbuck took a long cutting-spade pole, and with his knife slightly split the end, to insert the letter there, and in that way hand it to the boat without its having to come any closer to the ship.
Meanwhile, Ahab holding the letter, muttered, "Mr. Har — yes, Mr. Harry — a woman's handwriting — the man's wife, I'll wager — aye — Mr. Harry Macey, Ship Jeroboam — why, it's Macey, and he's dead!"
"Poor fellow! Poor fellow! And from his wife," sighed Mayhew. "But let me have it."
"No, keep it yourself," cried Gabriel to Ahab. "You are soon going that way."

"Curses strangle you!" yelled Ahab. "Captain Mayhew, stand by now to receive it." And taking the fatal letter from Starbuck's hands, he caught it in the slit of the pole and reached it out toward the boat. But as he did so, the oarsmen, expecting it, stopped rowing; the boat drifted a little toward the ship's stern; so that, as if by magic, the letter suddenly came level with Gabriel's eager hand. He clutched it in an instant, seized the boat-knife, and, impaling the letter on it, sent it, thus loaded, back into the ship. It fell at Ahab's feet. Then Gabriel shrieked out to his comrades to pull hard on their oars, and in that manner the mutinous boat rapidly shot away from the Pequod.
After this interlude, as the seamen went back to work on the whale's jacket, many strange things were hinted about this wild affair.

modern_da.title: Kapitel 71 — Jeroboams historie
paragraphs: Skib og brise blæste videre hånd i hånd, men brisen var hurtigere end skibet, og efter kort tid begyndte Pequod at gynge.

Snart viste kikkerten ud fra den fremmedes både og bemandede mastetoppe, at hun var et hvalfangerskib. Men hun lå så langt til luvart og bevægede sig så hurtigt forbi, tilsyneladende på vej til en anden fangstplads, at Pequod ikke havde noget håb om at nå hende. Så blev signalet hejst for at se, hvad svar der ville komme.

Det skal siges her, at ligesom krigsflådens skibe har de amerikanske hvalfangerskibe hver deres eget signal. Alle disse signaler er samlet i en bog, med de enkelte skibes navne ved, og hver kaptajn har et eksemplar. På den måde kan hvalfangerkaptajnerne kende hinanden ude på havet, selv på store afstande og uden større besvær.

Til sidst blev Pequods signal besvaret af, at den fremmede hejste sit eget, og det viste, at skibet var Jeroboam fra Nantucket. Hun drejede rårne, satte kurs ned mod os, kom op ved siden af Pequod i læ og sænkede en båd. Den kom snart nær; men da faldrebstrappen netop blev gjort klar efter Starbucks ordre for at tage imod den besøgende kaptajn, viftede den fremmede med hånden fra bådens agterstavn for at vise, at det slet ikke var nødvendigt. Det viste sig, at Jeroboam havde en ondartet epidemi om bord, og at Mayhew, hendes kaptajn, var bange for at smitte Pequods folk. For selv om han selv og hans bådbesætning var raske, og selv om hans skib lå et halvt geværskud væk med et uforgængeligt hav og en uforgængelig luft, der rullede og flød imellem, holdt han sig alligevel samvittighedsfuldt til landjordens frygtsomme karantæne og nægtede blankt at komme i direkte berøring med Pequod.

Men det forhindrede på ingen måde al samtale. Jeroboams båd holdt et par yards afstand til skibet og klarede med et åretag nu og da at holde sig parallelt med Pequod, mens hun tungt pløjede sig gennem søen (for nu blæste det ganske friskt), med stormarsesejlet bakket. Ganske vist skubbede en pludselig stor rullende bølge til tider båden et stykke frem, men den blev hurtigt dygtigt ført tilbage til sin rette plads. Med sådanne og andre afbrydelser nu og da blev der holdt en samtale i gang mellem de to parter — selv om den med mellemrum blev brudt af endnu en afbrydelse af en helt anden slags.

Ved en åre i Jeroboams båd sad en mand med et enestående udseende, selv i dette vilde fangstliv, hvor alt består af ikke andet end bemærkelsesværdige personer. Han var en lille, kort, ret ung mand, overstrøet med fregner i hele ansigtet og med en stor mængde gult hår. En langskødet frakke med et kabbalistisk snit, af en falmet valnøddebrun farve, indhyllede ham; dens overlappende ærmer var smøget op ved håndleddene. Der var et dybt, fast, fanatisk delirium i hans øjne.

Så snart denne skikkelse første gang var set, havde Stubb udbrudt — »Det er ham! Det er ham! — den langfrakkede skarnsmand, som Town-Hos folk fortalte os om!« Stubb tænkte her på en mærkelig historie, der var blevet fortalt om Jeroboam og en bestemt mand blandt hendes besætning, en tid forinden, da Pequod havde talt med Town-Ho. Ifølge denne beretning og det, man senere fik at vide, syntes den nævnte skarnsmand at have vundet et bemærkelsesværdigt tag i næsten alle på Jeroboam. Hans historie var denne:

Han var oprindelig vokset op blandt de skøre shakere i Neskyeuna, hvor han havde været en stor profet; på deres forskruede, hemmelige møder var han flere gange kommet ned fra himlen gennem en faldlem og havde forkyndt, at den syvende skål snart ville blive åbnet — den, han bar i vestelommen, men som i stedet for krudt skulle være ladet med laudanum. Grebet af et mærkeligt, apostolisk lune forlod han Neskyeuna for Nantucket, hvor han, med den snedighed, der er særegen for galskaben, tog et roligt, fornuftigt ydre på og meldte sig som uerfaren kandidat til Jeroboams fangstrejse. De tog ham ombord; men i det øjeblik skibet var ude af syne af land, brød hans sindssyge løs som en flod. Han udråbte sig selv til ærkeenglen Gabriel og befalede kaptajnen at springe over bord. Han udsendte sit manifest, hvor han erklærede sig for øernes befrier i havet og generalvikar for hele Oceanien. Den urokkelige alvor, hvormed han erklærede alt dette — det mørke, dristige spil i hans søvnløse, ophidsede fantasi og al den overnaturlige skræk fra et virkeligt delirium — gav tilsammen denne Gabriel en luft af hellighed i de fleste uvidende besætningsmedlemmers sind. Desuden var de bange for ham. Da sådan en mand ikke var til megen praktisk nytte på skibet, især da han nægtede at arbejde, undtagen når det passede ham, ville den vantro kaptajn gerne have været ham kvit. Men da ærkeenglen hørte, at kaptajnen agtede at sætte ham i land i den første belejlige havn, åbnede han straks alle sine segl og skåle — og lovede skibet og alle mand ubetinget fortabelse, hvis den hensigt blev ført ud i livet. Så stærkt påvirkede han sine disciple blandt besætningen, at de til sidst gik til kaptajnen alle sammen og sagde til ham, at hvis Gabriel blev sendt fra skibet, ville ikke en mand af dem blive tilbage. Han blev derfor tvunget til at opgive sin plan. De ville heller ikke tillade, at Gabriel blev mishandlet på nogen måde, hvad han end sagde eller gjorde; så det endte med, at Gabriel havde fuld frihed på skibet. Følgen af alt dette var, at ærkeenglen brød sig lidt eller slet ikke om kaptajnen og styrmændene; og siden epidemien var brudt ud, var han mere egenmægtig end nogensinde og erklærede, at pesten, som han kaldte den, stod helt og holdent til hans kommando, og at den ikke ville høre op, undtagen når det behagede ham. Sømændene, for det meste stakkels stakler, krøb for ham, og nogle af dem logrede for ham; efter hans anvisninger viste de ham nogle gange personlig hyldest som til en gud. Den slags kan synes utroligt; men hvor forbavsende det end er, så er det sandt. Og fanatikeres historie er heller ikke halvt så slående for fanatikerens egen grænseløse selvbedrag som for hans grænseløse magt til at bedrage og forhekse så mange andre. Men det er på tide at vende tilbage til Pequod.
»Jeg er ikke bange for jeres epidemi, mand,« sagde Ahab fra essingen til kaptajn Mayhew, som stod i bådens agterstavn. »Kom om bord.«
Men nu sprang Gabriel op.
»Tænk, tænk på feberne, de gule og de galdeagtige! Pas på den rædselsfulde pest!«
»Gabriel! Gabriel!« råbte kaptajn Mayhew. »Du må enten —« Men i det øjeblik skød en styrtende bølge båden langt frem, og dens larm druknede al tale.
»Har du set den hvide hval?« spurgte Ahab, da båden drev tilbage.
»Tænk, tænk på din hvalbåd, knust og sunket! Pas på den rædselsfulde hale!«

»Jeg siger dig igen, Gabriel, at —« Men endnu en gang skød båden frem, som om djævle trak i den. I nogle øjeblikke sagde ingen noget, mens en række vilde bølger rullede forbi — bølger, som i et af havets lejlighedsvise luner mere væltede båden rundt end løftede den. I mellemtiden slingrede det hejste kaskelothoved voldsomt, og man kunne se Gabriel kaste et ret ængsteligt blik på det, mere end hans ærkeengle-natur syntes at berettige.

Da dette mellemspil var forbi, begyndte kaptajn Mayhew på en mørk historie om Moby Dick — dog ikke uden hyppige afbrydelser fra Gabriel, hver gang hans navn blev nævnt, og fra det skøre hav, som syntes at være i ledtog med ham.

Det viste sig, at Jeroboam ikke havde været længe hjemmefra, da hendes folk, idet de talte med et hvalfangerskib, fik pålidelig besked om Moby Dicks eksistens og den ødelæggelse, han havde forvoldt. Gabriel drak grådigt denne nyhed i sig og advarede højtideligt kaptajnen mod at angribe den hvide hval, hvis uhyret skulle blive set; i sin pludrende sindssyge erklærede han, at den hvide hval ikke var mindre end shakernes Gud i kødet, eftersom shakerne tror på Bibelen. Men da Moby Dick et år eller to senere blev set med sikkerhed fra mastetoppene, brændte Macey, den første styrmand, af iver efter at møde ham; og da kaptajnen selv ikke var uvillig til at give ham chancen, trods alle ærkeenglens trusler og advarsler, lykkedes det Macey at overtale fem mand til at bemande hans båd. Med dem skød han fra skibet; og efter megen træls roning og mange farlige, mislykkede angreb lykkedes det ham til sidst at få ét jern til at sidde fast. I mellemtiden klatrede Gabriel op i storroyalstangens top og kastede med den ene arm i vanvittige fagter og slyngede profetier om hurtig undergang ud over dem, der helligbrødigt angreb hans guddom. Nu, mens Macey, styrmanden, stod oppe i bådens stævn og med al sin stammes hensynsløse energi udstødte vilde råb mod hvalen og prøvede at få en god chance for sin løftede lanse — se! en bred hvid skygge rejste sig fra havet, og med sin hurtige viftende bevægelse slog den for øjeblikket vejret ud af roernes kroppe. I næste øjeblik blev den uheldige styrmand, så fuld af rasende liv, slynget op i luften, og idet han faldt ned i en lang bue, ramte han havet omkring halvtreds yard væk. Ikke et splint af båden tog skade, ikke et hår på nogen roers hoved; men styrmanden sank for evigt.

Det er værd at tilføje her, i en parentes, at blandt de dødelige ulykker i kaskelotfangsten er denne slags måske næsten lige så almindelig som nogen. Nogle gange tager ingen skade andre end den mand, der bliver slået ud på den måde; oftere bliver bådens stævn slået af, eller lårbrættet, hvor bådføreren (den officer, der kommanderer båden) står, rives løs og følger med kroppen. Men det mærkeligste af alt er, at der mere end én gang ikke kunne findes et eneste spor af vold på kroppen, da den blev fundet — og alligevel var manden stendød.

Fra skibet var hele ulykken, med Maceys faldende krop, tydeligt at se. Med et gennemtrængende skrig — »Skålen! Skålen!« — kaldte Gabriel den rædselsslagne besætning tilbage fra enhver videre forfølgelse af hvalen. Denne forfærdelige begivenhed gav ærkeenglen endnu mere indflydelse, fordi hans lettroende disciple troede, at han havde forudsagt netop dette, og ikke blot havde udtalt en almindelig profeti, som hvem som helst kunne have gjort, og som så tilfældigvis traf et af de mange mål, dens brede margin tillod. Han blev en unævnelig skræk for skibet.

Da Mayhew var færdig med sin historie, stillede Ahab ham sådanne spørgsmål, at den fremmede kaptajn ikke kunne lade være med at spørge, om han agtede at jage den hvide hval, hvis lejligheden bød sig. Hvortil Ahab svarede — »Ja.« Straks sprang Gabriel endnu en gang op, stirrede på den gamle mand og udbrød heftigt med nedadpegende finger — »Tænk, tænk på blasfemikeren — død og dernede! — pas på blasfemikerens ende!«

Ahab vendte sig sejt til side og sagde så til Mayhew: »Kaptajn, jeg kom lige til at huske min brevpose. Der er et brev til en af jeres officerer, hvis jeg ikke tager fejl. Starbuck, kig posen igennem.«

Hvert hvalfangerskib har et godt antal breve med ud til forskellige andre skibe, og om de når frem til dem, de er stilet til, afhænger af ren tilfældighed, nemlig om man møder de skibe et sted på de fire have. Så de fleste breve når aldrig frem; og mange bliver først modtaget, når de er to eller tre år gamle eller mere.

Snart kom Starbuck tilbage med et brev i hånden. Det var slemt krøllet, fugtigt og dækket af en mat, plettet grøn skimmel af at have ligget i et mørkt skab i kahytten. Til sådan et brev kunne Døden selv godt have været postbud.

»Kan du ikke læse det?« råbte Ahab. »Giv mig det, mand. Ja, ja, det er kun utydelige kragetæer — hvad er det her?« Mens han studerede det, tog Starbuck en lang stang med en skærespade, flækkede enden lidt med sin kniv for at stikke brevet derind og på den måde række det til båden uden at den behøvede at komme nærmere skibet.

Imens mumlede Ahab, mens han holdt brevet: »Mr. Har — ja, Mr. Harry — en kvindes håndskrift — mandens kone, vil jeg vædde på — ja — Mr. Harry Macey, skibet Jeroboam — jamen det er jo Macey, og han er død!«
»Stakkels mand! Stakkels mand! Og fra hans kone,« sukkede Mayhew. »Men lad mig få det.«
»Nej, behold det selv,« råbte Gabriel til Ahab. »De skal snart den vej.«

»Forbandelsen kvæle dig!« brølede Ahab. »Kaptajn Mayhew, gør Dem klar til at modtage det.« Han tog det skæbnesvangre brev fra Starbucks hænder, stak det ind i spalten i stangen og rakte det ud mod båden. Men netop da holdt roerne, som havde ventet det, op med at ro. Båden drev lidt ind mod skibets hæk, så brevet som ved trolddom pludselig kom i højde med Gabriels grådige hånd. Han greb det på et øjeblik, tog bådkniven, spiddede brevet på den og sendte det således belæsset tilbage til skibet. Det faldt for Ahabs fødder. Så skreg Gabriel til sine kammerater, at de skulle trække hårdt i årerne, og på den måde skød den mytteriske båd hurtigt væk fra Pequod.
Efter dette mellemspil gik søfolkene tilbage til arbejdet med hvalens kappe, og der blev der antydet mange mærkelige ting om denne vilde affære.
